stimulus:
Eduardo Galeano's 'Open Veins of Latin America' (1971) — a blistering account of five centuries of foreign exploitation — was banned by the military dictatorships of Uruguay, Chile, and Argentina in the 1970s, even as it became a bestseller across the continent.

The bans tell their own story. Uruguay's dictatorship seized copies; Chile's junta burned them; Argentina's generals listed the book as subversive. Yet it circulated in samizdat and exile editions and became a sacred text of the Latin American left — Hugo Chávez famously handed a copy to Barack Obama in 2009. A book that dictatorships fear enough to ban has, in a sense, already proved its argument about how power works.
stem: The banning of Galeano's book by right-wing dictatorships suggests that they saw it as
options: (A) a work commissioned by foreign intelligence agencies
(B) a defense of colonialism
(C) a harmless cookbook
(D) A dangerous leftist critique
explanation: Dictatorships ban books they fear. 'Open Veins' argued that Latin America's poverty was the product of exploitation by foreign powers and local elites — an argument that legitimized resistance to the very regimes (often installed with foreign backing) that banned it.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The book attacked foreign intervention; it was not a product of it.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. It is one of the most famous anti-colonial texts of the 20th century.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. This trivializes a major work of political economy.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The bans confirm the book's perceived subversive power.

stimulus:
In 1954, Guatemala's reformist president Jacobo Árbenz was overthrown in a CIA-backed coup after his land reform expropriated unused lands of the United Fruit Company — the American corporation that dominated Guatemala's banana exports, railroads, and ports.

The company's power in Guatemala was the stuff of legend: it owned the railroads, the ports, the telegraphs, and vast banana lands — 'the octopus,' Guatemalans called it. When Árbenz's Decree 900 expropriated uncultivated company lands (with compensation in government bonds), United Fruit's lobbyists — with close ties to the Eisenhower administration — painted the reform as communist. The CIA's Operation PBSUCCESS toppled Árbenz in 1954, inaugurating decades of military rule and civil war.
stem: The United Fruit Company's interests were directly involved in which of the following?
options: (A) The 1954 CIA-backed coup in Guatemala
(B) The building of the Panama Canal under U.S. direction
(C) The Mexican Revolution
(D) The Cuban missile crisis
explanation: United Fruit — 'el pulpo,' the octopus — lobbied Washington hard against Árbenz, and the CIA's Operation PBSUCCESS restored a friendly regime. Guatemala became the textbook case of a corporation's interests driving U.S. intervention — exactly the dynamic Galeano denounced.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The 1954 coup is the classic United Fruit intervention.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The canal was a U.S. government project, not a UFCO operation.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Mexican Revolution (1910–1920) predates and lies outside this story.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The missile crisis (1962) involved Cuba and the USSR, not UFCO.

stimulus: World population reached 1 billion around 1800, 2 billion around 1930, 4 billion around 1975, and 6 billion around 1999 — with the time needed to add each billion shrinking dramatically.
stem: Demographers explain the pattern in the chart using
options: (A) The demographic transition model
(B) The Malthusian trap of overpopulation
(C) The theory of relativity in physics
(D) The theory of plate tectonics
explanation: The explosion happened because mortality collapsed first: better nutrition, sanitation, and medicine let far more children survive, while birth rates took generations to fall. That gap — deaths down, births still up — is the demographic transition's engine, and it produced the population surge.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The transition model explains the surge as a mortality-first phenomenon.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Malthus predicted catastrophe from overpopulation; the transition model explains why growth happened.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Relativity is physics, irrelevant to demography.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Plate tectonics is geology, irrelevant to demography.

stimulus: A chart of world population (1 CE–1999) shows accelerating global growth. Behind the global curve lie sharp regional differences: Europe's birth rates began falling in the late 1800s, while much of Asia, Africa, and Latin America maintained high birth rates deep into the 1900s.
stem: The chart's global figures mask important regional differences, such as
options: (A) Asia's population shrinking throughout the 1900s
(B) Africa having the slowest population growth of any continent by far
(C) Europe's birth rates falling earlier while developing regions kept growing
(D) the complete absence of any regional differences
explanation: The demographic transition did not happen everywhere at once. Europe and North America completed it first; the developing world entered the high-growth phase later and stayed in it longer. A single global curve averages together very different regional histories.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Asia's population grew enormously in the 1900s.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Africa had among the fastest growth rates.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Staggered transitions created the regional divergence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Regional differences in timing are among the most important facts in demography.

stimulus: World population reached 1 billion around 1800, 2 billion around 1930, 4 billion around 1975, and 6 billion around 1999. Each doubling arrived faster than the last, raising urgent questions about whether the planet's resources could sustain the growth.
stem: The trend shown has fueled debates about
options: (A) The causes of the last Ice Age
(B) The speed of light
(C) Earth's carrying capacity for humans
(D) Whether the moon is inhabited
explanation: Explosive population growth revived Malthusian anxieties in modern form: can the planet feed, house, and employ billions more without ecological collapse? The carrying-capacity debate — from 'The Population Bomb' to sustainable-development goals — is the direct intellectual child of this curve.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Ice Age causes belong to climatology and deep time.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The speed of light is a physics constant.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Population growth made carrying capacity a central global question.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The moon's habitability is unrelated to human demography.

stimulus: In 1998, the United States — with under 5 percent of the world's population — consumed about 94.6 quadrillion BTU of primary energy, roughly a quarter of the world total. China, with over a fifth of humanity, consumed about 33.9 quadrillion BTU.
stem: This disparity is most often used to illustrate
options: (A) The heavy consumption of wealthy industrialized nations
(B) American energy poverty
(C) the absence of industry in the United States
(D) the equal distribution of energy use across the world
explanation: The figures make the inequality concrete: a small fraction of humanity using a huge fraction of the energy. Environmental debates return to this ratio constantly — it underlies arguments about who bears responsibility for climate change and who should cut consumption first.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The data quantifies the consumption gap between rich and poor nations.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The U.S. figures show abundance, not poverty.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. High energy use reflects extensive industry, not its absence.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The figures demonstrate extreme inequality, not equality.

stimulus: A 1998 chart ranks the world's top energy consumers: the United States first by far, followed by China, Russia, Japan, and Germany. The chart appeared one year after the Kyoto Protocol, the first international treaty to set binding limits on greenhouse-gas emissions.
stem: The Kyoto Protocol of 1997
options: (A) Regulation of ocean fishing rights
(B) Binding targets for developed nations, rejected by the Senate
(C) A total worldwide ban on energy use
(D) An agreement signed by every nation including the United States
explanation: Kyoto required industrialized nations to cut emissions below 1990 levels — but exempted developing nations like China and India, and the United States, the largest emitter, never ratified it. The treaty's fate shows how the energy-consumption hierarchy in the chart translated into diplomatic deadlock.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Kyoto concerned greenhouse gases, not fishing.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Kyoto's binding targets, developing-nation exemptions, and U.S. non-ratification define its history.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Kyoto limited emissions growth; it did not ban energy use.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The United States never ratified the Kyoto Protocol.

stimulus: A 1998 chart ranks the world's top energy consumers: the United States first by far, followed by China, Russia, Japan, and Germany. China ranked second despite having a far lower per-capita income than any other country on the list.
stem: China's high ranking on the chart despite its lower level of development shows
options: (A) that the chart measures military spending
(B) that per-capita data is never useful
(C) Population size as well as wealth
(D) that China was the richest country in the world
explanation: Total energy use is population times per-person use. China's billion-plus people multiplied even modest per-capita consumption into a world-scale total — which is why populous developing nations loom so large in climate politics despite their poverty.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The chart measures energy consumption, not military budgets.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Per-capita data is essential; it answers a different question than totals do.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Population scale explains China's position on a totals chart.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. China was still a low-income country in 1998.

stimulus: Two images: a Japanese woodcut of musket-armed troops from the late 1500s, and a photograph of Senegalese soldiers in French uniforms carrying modern rifles, c. 1900. Both show non-Europeans wielding gunpowder weapons.
stem: The two images differ in that
options: (A) Both images show the same army
(B) Japan by trade; Senegal by colonial service
(C) both images show Europeans using the weapons
(D) neither image involves gunpowder weapons
explanation: Same technology, opposite power relations. Japan acquired muskets from Portuguese traders in 1543 and had them copied by Japanese smiths within years — adoption by a sovereign state. The Senegalese tirailleurs were issued French rifles as subjects of an empire — adoption through subordination. The contrast shows technology transfer serving very different political structures.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The images show Japanese and Senegalese forces three centuries apart.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Voluntary adoption versus colonial issue is the key difference.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Both images show non-European troops.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Muskets and rifles are gunpowder weapons in both images.

stimulus: A Japanese woodcut from the late 1500s shows foot soldiers armed with muskets — weapons introduced by Portuguese traders in 1543 and quickly copied by Japanese gunsmiths. A century later, under the Tokugawa shogunate, firearms had all but vanished from Japanese warfare.
stem: Under the Tokugawa shogunate, Japan famously
options: (A) forgot the existence of gunpowder entirely
(B) restricted firearms to preserve the samurai social order
(C) armed every peasant with a musket
(D) became the world's leading exporter of guns worldwide
explanation: Historian Noel Perrin's 'giving up the gun' thesis: the Tokugawa, having unified Japan, saw firearms as a threat to the sword-bearing samurai elite and to domestic peace. By restricting guns to ceremonial use, they froze the military technology that had helped win the civil wars — a political choice, not a technological failure.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Gunsmiths and knowledge persisted; use was restricted, not forgotten.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Tokugawa gun control protected the samurai-centered social order.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Arming peasants was exactly what the shogunate wanted to prevent.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Japan exported little weaponry in this period.

stimulus: A photograph shows Senegalese tirailleurs — African infantrymen in French service — in uniform with modern rifles, c. 1900. France recruited tens of thousands of West Africans into its colonial army.
stem: The troops shown were used extensively by France
options: (A) As front-line soldiers in World War I
(B) only as military musicians
(C) never outside the borders of Senegal
(D) as admirals of the French fleet
explanation: Some 200,000 tirailleurs sénégalais served in World War I — at Verdun, the Somme, and Chemin des Dames — with tens of thousands killed. France called it the 'blood tax': colonial subjects paying for empire with their lives, a sacrifice later generations would invoke when demanding citizenship and independence.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The tirailleurs' WWI service and losses are well documented.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. They were combat infantry, not bandsmen.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. They were shipped to European battlefields.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. They were army infantry, not naval officers.

stimulus: A photograph shows Senegalese tirailleurs in French service, c. 1900. After African independence in the 1960s, many veterans discovered that France had frozen their military pensions at 1959 levels — worth a fraction of what French veterans received.
stem: After decolonization, many African veterans of the French army faced
options: (A) Frozen pensions far lower than French veterans'
(B) immediate promotion to the rank of general
(C) universal celebration with no unresolved issues
(D) conscription into the British army
explanation: The 1959 'cristallisation' froze colonial veterans' pensions while French veterans' pensions kept rising with inflation. Men who had bled for France at Verdun received a pittance — a postcolonial injustice that took until the 2000s to begin to redress, and a bitter memory across francophone Africa.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Pension inequality became a symbol of colonialism's unpaid debts.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Veterans were marginalized, not promoted.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The pension issue festered for decades.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. They had served France, not Britain.

stimulus:
In 1804, the Islamic scholar Usman dan Fodio proclaimed a jihad in what is now northern Nigeria, denouncing the Hausa kings for corruption, unjust taxation, and un-Islamic practices. His followers overthrew the Hausa states and founded the Sokoto Caliphate.

The accusation was specific: the Hausa kings levied taxes Islam did not sanction, mixed Islamic observance with local custom, and — in dan Fodio's telling — oppressed Muslim scholars and commoners alike. The jihad was thus framed as reform, not conquest: a return to proper Islam against rulers who were Muslim in name only. It was fellow Muslims, not outsiders, who were the primary target.
stem: The jihad proclaimed in the passage was directed mainly against
options: (A) Buddhist kingdoms
(B) Hausa rulers accused of corruption
(C) European colonizers of the later 1800s
(D) the Ottoman Empire
explanation: Dan Fodio's jihad was a reform movement within the Islamic world: a scholar's revolt against Muslim rulers he judged impious and oppressive. It was not anti-colonial (the British came a century later) but a bid to purify Islamic government from within.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. There were no Buddhist kingdoms in West Africa.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The jihad targeted the Hausa kingdoms, especially Gobir.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Europeans had not yet colonized the region in 1804.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Ottomans were far away and irrelevant to this struggle.

stimulus:
Usman dan Fodio's 1804 jihad founded the Sokoto Caliphate in what is now northern Nigeria — a state that at its height governed some 10 million people across a vast territory, with a bureaucracy, courts, schools, and a celebrated tradition of Islamic scholarship.

The caliphate's administration was run by a literate elite: qadis applied Islamic law in the courts, emirs governed provinces, and a celebrated scholarly tradition — including the writings of dan Fodio's daughter Nana Asma'u, who organized women's education — made Sokoto a center of Islamic learning. It was among the largest states in nineteenth-century Africa, and its institutions survived its conquest: the British preserved the emirate system under indirect rule after 1903.
stem: The state founded by this jihad became
options: (A) a single small village
(B) a European colony within a decade
(C) a maritime empire in Southeast Asia
(D) A huge 19th-century African empire
explanation: Sokoto was among the great states of 19th-century Africa — a theocratic empire with provinces, judges, tax collectors, and scholars like Nana Asma'u, dan Fodio's daughter. It survived until the British conquest of 1903, nearly a century after its founding.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. It was a vast multi-ethnic empire, not a village.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. British conquest came in 1903, a century later.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Sokoto was a land empire in West Africa.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The Sokoto Caliphate's scale and durability were remarkable.

stimulus:
Usman dan Fodio's 1804 jihad in West Africa proclaimed a purified Islamic state under a caliph uniting religious and political authority. Half a century later, al-Hajj Umar Tall launched a similar Islamic reform jihad in the same region, likewise denouncing corrupt rulers and founding a new state.

Al-Hajj Umar Tall's jihad (1850s–1860s) in the Senegal valley followed the same script: denunciation of corrupt rulers, proclamation of a purified Islamic state, and military expansion under a leader uniting spiritual and temporal authority. Both movements belong to the great nineteenth-century wave of Islamic reform jihads across West Africa — responses to the perceived decay of Muslim rulership and the first pressures of European encroachment.
stem: The movement described is most similar to which of the following?
options: (A) Other West African reform jihads
(B) The Protestant Reformation in Europe
(C) The Meiji Restoration in Japan
(D) The Russian Revolution of 1917
explanation: West Africa saw a whole age of reform jihads — dan Fodio's Sokoto, Umar's Tukulor empire, Samori Touré's state — each led by scholars claiming to restore pure Islam against corrupt rulers. They form a distinct regional pattern of Islamic state-building in the 19th century.

option_explanations.A: Correct. The jihads belong to a shared West African reform tradition.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The Reformation was a Christian movement in 16th-century Europe.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Meiji Restoration was Japan's modernizing revolution, not an Islamic jihad.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The Russian Revolution was secular and socialist.

stimulus: An 18th-century engraving shows Chinese silk workshops: rows of workers reeling silk, operating looms, and organizing production in large households that sold their cloth to distant markets — manufacturing without factories.
stem: Protoindustrialization, illustrated by the image, refers to
options: (A) Rural household manufacturing for distant markets
(B) the invention of the steam engine
(C) large mechanized factories in industrial cities
(D) the end of all craft production
explanation: Before industrialization, much of the world's manufacturing happened in homes and workshops — rural families spinning, weaving, and reeling for merchants who sold across regions. This 'protoindustry' built the commercial networks, skills, and capital that later fed factory industrialization.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Household production for markets is the definition of protoindustrialization.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The steam engine belongs to industrialization proper, which came later.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Factories are what protoindustrialization precedes.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Protoindustrialization expanded craft production; it did not end it.

stimulus: An 18th-century English engraving, 'The Silk Manufacture in China,' depicts Chinese workshops with sophisticated machinery for reeling and weaving silk. The engraving was based on detailed reports sent home by Jesuit missionaries living in China.
stem: The image's origin in Jesuit missionary reports suggests
options: (A) Keen European interest in Chinese technology
(B) the image is a photograph
(C) Jesuit missionaries never actually went to China
(D) England had no interest in Chinese goods or techniques
explanation: The Jesuits were Europe's window into China, and their admiring reports on Chinese science, machinery, and administration fed a European fascination — chinoiserie in art, and serious study of Chinese techniques. An England eagerly illustrating Chinese silk machinery is not an England that considered China stagnant.

option_explanations.A: Correct. Jesuit transmission shows active European engagement with Chinese know-how.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Photography did not exist in the 1700s; this is an engraving.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Jesuits were the most famous European residents of Ming-Qing China.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The engraving itself proves English interest.

stimulus: In the 1700s, China sold Europe enormous quantities of silk, tea, and porcelain while buying almost nothing in return. The difference was paid in silver — much of it mined in the Americas — which flowed into China in staggering quantities.
stem: China's persistent trade surplus meant that in the 1700s China
options: (A) used only paper money and no silver
(B) refused to accept any foreign goods at all, including silver
(C) Absorbed vast New World silver, becoming a global 'silver sink'
(D) exported silver to Europe
explanation: China's economy ran on silver — taxes were paid in it — and the trade surplus sucked in perhaps half the New World's silver output. The 'silver sink' is one of early modern history's great facts: American mines, European merchants, and Chinese demand linked in a single global circuit.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Silver was central to the Ming-Qing monetary system.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Silver was the one foreign good China accepted eagerly.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Silver flowed overwhelmingly one way: into China.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. China imported silver; it did not export it.

stimulus: Ghana's Kwame Nkrumah told fellow African leaders: 'Is it not unity alone that can weld us into an effective force?' In 1963, his vision produced the Organization of African Unity, founded in Addis Ababa — though as a loose association of sovereign states, not the continental union government he had wanted.
stem: Nkrumah's vision led most directly to the creation of
options: (A) the European Union
(B) NATO
(C) The Organization of African Unity (1963)
(D) A single African superstate with one president
explanation: The OAU was the compromise between Nkrumah's dream of political union and other leaders' insistence on sovereignty. It gave Africa a continental voice — against apartheid, for decolonization — while leaving real power with the member states. Nkrumah got the organization; he did not get the union.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The EU is a European institution, unrelated to Nkrumah.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. NATO is a Cold War military alliance.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The OAU institutionalized Pan-Africanism in diluted form.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. No continental superstate was ever created.

stimulus:
Kwame Nkrumah demanded rapid continental political union for Africa. Many fellow leaders — the 'Monrovia group' — preferred to move slowly, building economic cooperation first while guarding the sovereignty their nations had just won.

The Monrovia group's caution was born of recent experience: their nations had just won sovereignty after long struggles, and they were reluctant to surrender it to a new continental authority. They preferred functional cooperation — trade, development, diplomacy — through the Organization of African Unity (1963), which enshrined non-interference in members' internal affairs. Nkrumah's union government never materialized; the OAU's loose confederal model won.
stem: Nkrumah's call for continental union was opposed by leaders who favored
options: (A) immediate world government
(B) recolonization by European powers
(C) a close military union with the Soviet Union
(D) Gradual cooperation preserving national sovereignty
explanation: Newly independent states were jealous of the sovereignty they had just won; few wanted to surrender it to Accra or Addis Ababa. The gradualists' victory shaped African institutions for decades: cooperation without surrender of independence — the OAU's founding principle.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. No African leader proposed world government.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Recolonization was no one's program.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. Soviet military union was never on the table.
option_explanations.D: Correct. Gradualism and sovereignty won out over Nkrumah's maximalism.

stimulus:
Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's founding president and the great prophet of Pan-African unity, was overthrown in a military coup in February 1966 while on a state visit to Vietnam. Economic crisis, authoritarian measures, and the creation of a one-party state had eroded his once-vast popularity.

The coup of February 24, 1966 was greeted with celebration in Accra — and with suspicion abroad, where many assumed CIA involvement. Nkrumah spent his final years in exile in Guinea, still writing and still preaching continental union. Ghana cycled through military and civilian governments for the next fifteen years. The prophet of Pan-Africanism lived to see his own country reject him and his continental dream deferred.
stem: Nkrumah was overthrown in 1966 while
options: (A) Personally leading troops in battle
(B) Resisting a French invasion of Ghana
(C) Dying peacefully in office of old age at home
(D) Abroad, as troubles at home eroded his support
explanation: The liberator became the autocrat: Nkrumah's grandiose projects drained the treasury, his Preventive Detention Act jailed opponents, and the army — backed quietly by Western intelligence — struck while he was in Hanoi. His fall is the classic arc of the independence-era strongman.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. He was a politician, not a battlefield commander, and was abroad when deposed.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. There was no French invasion of Ghana.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. He was deposed in 1966 and died in exile in 1972.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The 1966 coup ended Nkrumah's rule during his Vietnam trip.

stimulus: A world map shows European colonial claims in the 1600s–1700s: Spain holds most of South and Central America plus the Philippines; Portugal holds Brazil and scattered coastal forts in Africa and Asia; France, England, and the Netherlands hold smaller coastal settlements and Caribbean islands.
stem: The map shows Spain's colonial holdings dwarfing those of other powers. This pattern mainly reflects
options: (A) an error by the mapmaker
(B) Spain's century-long head start, beginning in the 1490s
(C) Spain's overwhelming naval superiority in the 1700s
(D) other powers' complete lack of interest in colonization
explanation: Spain and Portugal divided the non-European world between them in the 1490s and had a hundred years' head start before England, France, and the Netherlands built serious overseas empires. The map's imbalance is a time-lag made visible: first movers held the most territory.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. The pattern is historically accurate, not a cartographic error.
option_explanations.B: Correct. The chronological head start explains the territorial imbalance.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. By the 1700s Britain and France rivaled or surpassed Spanish naval power.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. The other powers were intensely interested — they arrived later and took what remained.

stimulus: A world map shows European colonial claims in the 1600s–1700s: vast claimed territories, but actual European control mostly confined to coastlines, ports, and islands — with the interiors of Africa and Asia still governed by independent states.
stem: Despite their naval technology, Europeans in this era generally could not conquer the interiors of Africa and Asia because
options: (A) They possessed no ships
(B) International law forbade inland conquest
(C) They preferred to colonize the Arctic
(D) Disease and strong states kept them on the coasts
explanation: Gunboats could bombard a port but not march inland: malaria and other diseases killed Europeans in droves, supply lines stretched impossibly thin, and states like the Mughals, Ottomans, and Ashanti were formidable military powers. The map's coastal pattern shows the real limits of early modern European power.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. European naval technology was precisely their advantage.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. No such law existed; the limits were practical, not legal.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. The Arctic was not a colonial priority.
option_explanations.D: Correct. The coastal-enclave pattern reflects genuine constraints on European power.

stimulus: A world map shows European colonial claims in the 1600s–1700s, with the Caribbean dotted by the sugar islands of the Spanish, French, English, and Dutch — small territories that generated enormous wealth.
stem: The sugar economy of the Caribbean depended on
options: (A) Indigenous volunteers
(B) automated machinery
(C) enslaved African labor on plantations
(D) free European wage workers paid by the day
explanation: Sugar was brutal work — planting, cutting, and boiling cane around the clock in killing heat — and the plantation system ran on enslaved Africans, imported by the millions. The Caribbean sugar islands were the economic heart of the Atlantic slave system.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. Indigenous populations had been decimated; the labor force was African.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Mechanization came much later; this was hand labor.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Enslaved labor was the foundation of the Caribbean sugar economy.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Europeans would not do this work for wages; planters used enslaved labor instead.

stimulus:
In 1790, France's National Assembly decreed that 'all free citizens' of the colonies — including free men of color born of free parents — would enjoy political rights. Slavery itself was left untouched. In Saint-Domingue, the mixed-race leader Vincent Ogé demanded the decree be enforced.

The decree of March 8, 1790 was the National Assembly's attempt to square revolutionary principles with colonial interests. It declared that 'every person' over twenty-five owning property was an active citizen — language that free men of color, many of them wealthy planters and slaveholders themselves, seized upon. White colonists insisted the decree had never been meant for them; the Assembly, unwilling to choose between its principles and its colonies, issued vague 'clarifications' that satisfied no one.
stem: The National Assembly's instructions of March 8, 1790 granted political rights to
options: (A) only white colonists
(B) no one in the colonies
(C) Free men of color
(D) all enslaved people immediately
explanation: The March 8 decree was a halfway measure: it extended the Revolution's rights to wealthy free people of color — many of them slaveholders themselves — while carefully preserving slavery. That contradiction — liberty for some, chains for others — is what made Saint-Domingue explode.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. White colonists already had rights; the decree's novelty was its inclusion of free coloreds.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. The decree was real and was proclaimed in the colonies.
option_explanations.C: Correct. The decree enfranchised free men of color but protected slavery.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Abolition did not come until 1794, under wartime pressure.

stimulus:
Vincent Ogé, a wealthy mixed-race merchant of Saint-Domingue, demanded that white colonists implement the National Assembly's 1790 decree granting rights to free men of color. When they refused, he raised an armed revolt — and was captured, tortured, and broken on the wheel in February 1791.

Ogé had lobbied in Paris for the rights of free coloreds before returning to Saint-Domingue to demand the March decree's enforcement. Refused by the governor, he raised some 300 armed followers in October 1790. The revolt was quickly crushed, and in February 1791 Ogé and his lieutenant Chavannes were broken on the wheel — a deliberately gruesome public execution meant to terrorize free coloreds into submission. It had the opposite effect: it convinced them, and soon the enslaved, that nothing would be won without force.
stem: Ogé was executed in 1791 after
options: (A) being appointed governor of the colony
(B) Leading an armed revolt against the colonists
(C) voluntarily surrendering and receiving a pardon
(D) fleeing to Spanish territory
explanation: Ogé's rebellion failed, but his execution radicalized the colony: it showed free people of color that peaceful demands would be answered with the wheel. Months later, the enslaved rose in the great insurrection of August 1791 — the opening of the Haitian Revolution.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. He was a rebel, not an officeholder.
option_explanations.B: Correct. Ogé's revolt and brutal execution are the prologue to the Haitian Revolution.
option_explanations.C: Wrong. He received no pardon; he was executed with exemplary cruelty.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. He was captured, not exiled.

stimulus:
In August 1791, enslaved people across northern Saint-Domingue rose in a coordinated insurrection. Tradition holds that the revolt was planned at a vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman, led by the maroon leader Dutty Boukman — the beginning of the Haitian Revolution.

The uprising of August 1791 was meticulously planned: enslaved leaders coordinated across plantations, and on the night of August 14 a vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman — led by the maroon Dutty Boukman — sealed the conspiracy. Within weeks northern Saint-Domingue was in flames; within two years the French Republic, desperate for soldiers, abolished slavery; within thirteen, Haiti was independent. The ceremony at Bois Caïman is remembered as the night the largest slave revolt in history began.
stem: The great enslaved uprising that followed Ogé's execution began in August 1791 at
options: (A) London, where Parliament debated colonial policy
(B) Madrid, seat of the Spanish Empire
(C) Bois Caïman, with a ceremony led by Boukman
(D) Paris, where the National Assembly met
explanation: Bois Caïman is Haiti's founding myth and historical anchor: the night the enslaved conspired to rise, launching a thirteen-year revolution that would destroy slavery and create the first Black republic. From Ogé's wheel to Boukman's ceremony, 1791 was the year Saint-Domingue became Haiti.

option_explanations.A: Wrong. London was not the site of the uprising.
option_explanations.B: Wrong. Madrid was not the site of the uprising.
option_explanations.C: Correct. Bois Caïman marks the start of the Haitian Revolution.
option_explanations.D: Wrong. Paris debated; Saint-Domingue acted.
